newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Gulf War reparations body to assess oil claims.
newsitem.headline: Gulf War reparations body to assess oil claims.

text.p: Billions of dollars in claims filed against Iraq by at least 60 oil companies will be assessed by a panel of judges approved on Tuesday, the U.N. Gulf War reparations body said.
The Governing Council of the United Nations Compensation Commission (UNCC), which ended a two-day meeting, also appointed a panel to review 2,750 Kuwaiti private sector corporate claims.

It also approved claims worth $720 million filed by 76,000 people in 43 countries who had proved losses of up to $100,000 directly due to Iraq's 1990-91 invasion and occupation of Kuwait, according to a statement by the Geneva-based fund.

But the ruling body, composed of the same 15 countries as the Security Council, delayed payment of $550 million to 220,000 Gulf War victims following Iraq's interruption of its oil sales under the oil-for-food deal, according to the UNCC's executive secretary Jean-Claude Aime.
"We will not be making the payments in August as scheduled because of the decision by the Iraqis to suspend oil exports," Aime told Reuters after the closed-door talks.
"We will have to postpone it either to September or October depending on the date Iraqis will resume oil exports," he added.
The UNCC receives 30 per cent of the revenue (or $100 million a month) from the limited sale of Iraqi crude oil, which the Security Council extended on June 4 for another six months.
The $2 billion deal aims to ease the plight of Iraqi civilians under crippling U.N. sanctions for nearly seven years.

But Baghdad has yet to complete its version of the aid distribution plan necessary for restarting the oil sales. U.N. officials must receive the plan for review and approval before sales can start. Iraq must also submit a pricing formula.

On Monday, a senior U.N. aid official said Iraq was at least one week away from finishing its aid plan. Traders suspect Baghdad may hold back oil sales as a tit-for-tat move to protest against U.S. blocks on food and medicine contracts.
Last week, a top Iraqi official in New York said the $800 million sitting in an escrow account from first round of oil sales must be exhausted before new sales start.
About 60 oil firms have filed claims in Geneva, according to diplomats familiar with a confidential UNCC report.
Last December the fund approved an award of $610 million to the Kuwait Oil Company (KOC) for the cost of putting out fires in hundreds of oil wells set alight during the Gulf War.
The same three-member arbitration panel which assessed the KOC claim, headed by Alan Philip of Denmark, was assigned the overall oil sector claims on Tuesday.
In its statement, the reparations fund also said the ruling body discussed how to speed up processing of claims of nearly $200 billion dollars in corporate and government claims.
"The Council has asked us to go back to the drawing board and submit a report in September on how to expedite the process," Aime said.
"Everyone wants us to expedite the process. The question is the time-frame," he added.
Western diplomats said the United States and others want the UNCC to speed up processing and complete work in five years -- instead of the 15-20 years it would take at the current pace.

In a speech on Monday, Khaled Al-Mudaf, the new chairman of Kuwait's Public Authority for Assessment of Compensation for Damages Resulting from the Iraqi Aggression (PAAC), welcomed payments already made by the fund to some individual claimants.

He called for "redoubling the efforts" to complete the review and processing of claims by individuals for losses of more than $100,000 (known as D claims), corporate claims (E claims) and government claims (F claims).
